l: Jerusalem, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: Jerusalem is taken, its houses rifled and its women ravished, and half the city goes into captivity while the rest remain. Afterward living waters flow out from it, it is lifted up and dwells safely with no more curse, and nations come there to worship. Every pot in it becomes holy to the LORD of Armies.

l: nations, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: All nations are gathered against Jerusalem to battle and take the city. The LORD fights them, and their peoples are struck by a plague and panic, and their wealth is gathered by Judah. Survivors must go up year to year to worship the King and keep the feast of booths, or no rain falls on them.

l: Mount of Olives, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: The Mount of Olives lies before Jerusalem on the east and is where the LORD's feet stand in that day. It splits in two from east to west, half moving north and half south, making a very great valley by which the people flee.

l: Judah, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: Judah also fights at Jerusalem in that day. The wealth of the surrounding nations, gold, silver and clothing, is gathered in great abundance. Every pot in Judah becomes holy to the LORD of Armies.

l: plague on the peoples, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: The LORD strikes all the peoples who fought against Jerusalem with a plague in which their flesh, eyes and tongues consume away while they stand. A great panic leads each to seize and raise his hand against his neighbor. A like plague falls on the horse, mule, camel, donkey and all animals in their camps.

l: feast of booths, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: The survivors of the nations that came against Jerusalem are to go up yearly to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, and keep the feast of booths. Nations that do not go up receive no rain, which is called the plague and punishment for failing to keep it.

l: Egypt, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: Egypt is singled out as an example among the families of the earth: if its family does not go up to Jerusalem, no rain will fall on it. This is called the punishment of Egypt, shared with all nations that do not go up to keep the feast of booths.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Zechariah, Chapter 14
s: The day of the LORD is announced as a day when plunder is divided within Jerusalem, and as a unique day known to the LORD, neither day nor night, with light at evening time. On it there is no light, cold or frost, living waters flow from Jerusalem, and the LORD is King over all the earth. It also brings the final battle, the plague on the nations, and the holiness of all things in Jerusalem and Judah.

l: The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: In Malachi chapter 1, the LORD tells Israel through Malachi that he has loved them, and when they ask how, he points to his love for Jacob over his brother Esau, whose mountains he made a desolation. Edom says it will rebuild, but the LORD of Armies says he will throw down what they build, and they will be called 'The Wicked Land.' The LORD then rebukes the priests for despising his name by offering polluted bread and blind, lame, and sick animals on his altar, which they would not dare present to their governor. He declares that he has no pleasure in them and will not accept their offerings, while his name is great among the nations, with pure offerings made everywhere. The chapter closes with a curse on the deceiver who vows a good male from his flock but sacrifices a defective one to the LORD, the great King.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: The LORD declares his love for Israel and cites his choice of Jacob over Esau as evidence. He rebukes the priests for despising his name and polluting his altar, says he has no pleasure in them and will not accept their offerings, and states that his name is great among the nations. He curses the deceiver who sacrifices a defective animal and calls himself a great King.

l: Israel, The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: Israel is addressed by the LORD through Malachi and told that he has loved them, though they ask how. They are told they will see the LORD's treatment of Edom and say that the LORD is great even beyond the border of Israel.

l: Jacob, The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: Jacob is named as Esau's brother and as the one the LORD loved. His case is the LORD's answer to Israel's question about how he has loved them.

l: Esau, The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: Esau is identified as Jacob's brother, yet the LORD says he hated him. The LORD made Esau's mountains a desolation and gave his heritage to the jackals of the wilderness.

l: Edom, The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: Edom says it has been beaten down but will return and build the waste places. The LORD of Armies replies that they may build but he will throw down, and they will be called 'The Wicked Land,' the people against whom the LORD shows wrath forever.

l: priests (the LORD's priests addressed), The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: The priests are accused of despising the LORD's name by offering polluted bread on his altar and calling his table contemptible. They are also said to offer blind, lame, and sick animals, to sniff at the service as a weariness, and to bring what was taken by violence. The LORD says he has no pleasure in them and will not accept an offering from their hand.

l: sacrifices (defective offerings), The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi / Chapter 1
s: Offerings of blind, lame, and sick animals are called evil, and the LORD asks whether a governor would accept such gifts. He rejects them, contrasting them with the pure offering made to his name among the nations. He curses the deceiver who vows a male from his flock but sacrifices a defective thing.

l: The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 2
s: In Chapter 2, the LORD of Armies addresses the priests, warning that he will send a curse on them and rebuke their offspring if they do not take his commandment to heart and honor his name. He contrasts them with Levi, with whom his covenant of life and peace stood, who revered him, taught true law, and turned many from iniquity. The priests have turned from the path, caused many to stumble in the law, and corrupted the covenant of Levi, so they have been made contemptible before the people. The text then turns to Judah and Israel, who deal treacherously against one another, profane the covenant by marrying the daughter of a foreign god, and face being cut off. The LORD also rejects offerings covered with tears because of faithlessness to the wife of one's youth, condemns hating and divorcing, and charges the people with wearying him by claiming evildoers are good in his sight.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 2
s: The LORD of Armies commands the priests to give glory to his name and threatens to curse their blessings and rebuke their offspring if they refuse. He recalls his covenant with Levi, vows to cut off those who profane holiness, and no longer regards or receives offerings from those who deal treacherously. He is witness between a man and the wife of his youth, declares that one who hates and divorces covers his garment with violence, and is wearied by people's words that call evildoers good and ask where the God of justice is.

l: priests (the LORD's priests addressed), The Book of Malachi, Chapter 2
s: The priests are told that if they do not listen or take the commandment to heart, the LORD will curse them and their blessings, rebuke their offspring, and spread dung from their feasts on their faces. They have turned from the path, caused many to stumble in the law, corrupted the covenant of Levi, and shown respect for persons in the law. As a result the LORD has made them contemptible and wicked before all the people.

l: Levi, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 2
s: Levi had a covenant of life and peace with the LORD, was reverent, and stood in awe of his name. The law of truth was in his mouth and no unrighteousness was in his lips; he walked with the LORD in peace and uprightness and turned many away from iniquity. He serves as the model of a priest whose lips keep knowledge.

l: covenant of Levi, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 2
s: The covenant of Levi is the LORD's covenant of life and peace given to Levi so that he would be reverent. The priests are accused of having corrupted it by turning from the path and causing many to stumble in the law. The commandment is sent so that this covenant may be with Levi.

l: Judah, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 2
s: Judah is said to have dealt treacherously, committing an abomination in Israel and Jerusalem. It has profaned the holiness of the LORD, whom it loves, by marrying the daughter of a foreign god. The LORD will cut off the man who does this from the tents of Jacob, even if he offers an offering to the LORD of Armies.

l: wife of your youth, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 2
s: The wife of your youth is described as a man's companion and the wife of his covenant, against whom men have dealt treacherously. The LORD has been witness between them and her husband. The people are told to take heed to their spirit and not deal treacherously against her, since hating and divorcing covers a man's garment with violence.

l: The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: In this chapter the LORD of Armies announces that he will send a messenger to prepare the way before him, followed by the sudden coming of the Lord to his temple. His coming is likened to a refiner's fire and launderers' soap, purifying the sons of Levi so that the offerings of Judah and Jerusalem will again please him, and he promises swift judgment on sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, and those who oppress workers, widows, orphans, and foreigners. Because the LORD does not change, the sons of Jacob are not consumed, and he calls them to return to him, charging that the nation robs him in tithes and offerings and is cursed. He invites them to bring the whole tithe into the storehouse and test him, promising overflowing blessing, protection of their crops, and that all nations will call them blessed. The people's harsh words that serving God is vain and that the proud and wicked prosper are answered by the account of those who feared the LORD, whose names are written in a book of memory and who will be spared as his own possession.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: The LORD of Armies announces that he will send a messenger, come suddenly to his temple, and act as a refiner to purify the sons of Levi. He declares that he does not change, calls the people to return to him, and promises to be a swift witness against wrongdoers. He invites the people to test him in the tithe, promising blessing, and he listens to those who fear him, writes a book of memory for them, and will spare them as his own possession.

l: messenger (the messenger who prepares the way), The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: The LORD says he will send a messenger who will prepare the way before him. The messenger is also called the messenger of the covenant, whom the people desire and who is said to be coming.

l: sons of Levi, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: The sons of Levi will be purified and refined like gold and silver by the LORD, who sits as a refiner and purifier. As a result they will offer offerings to the LORD in righteousness.

l: wrongdoers (sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers, oppressors), The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: The LORD says he will come near in judgment and be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers. The same judgment falls on those who oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, who deprive the foreigner of justice, and who do not fear him.

l: Israelite nation (the addressed people), The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: The people, called the sons of Jacob, are not consumed because the LORD does not change, though they have turned from his ordinances since the days of their fathers. They are told to return to him, are accused of robbing him in tithes and offerings and are called cursed, and are promised blessing if they bring the whole tithe. They are also rebuked for saying that serving God is vain and that the proud and wicked prosper, and they are told they will again discern between the righteous and the wicked.

l: tithes and offerings, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: The LORD charges that the nation robs him in tithes and offerings, bringing a curse on the whole nation. He commands that the whole tithe be brought into the storehouse so there is food in his house, promising to open the windows of heaven, pour out blessing, and rebuke the devourer so crops and vines do not fail. The offering of Judah and Jerusalem will again be pleasant to him as in ancient years.

l: those who fear the LORD's name, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: Those who feared the LORD spoke with one another, and the LORD listened and heard, and a book of memory was written before him for them and for those who honored his name. He says they shall be his own possession in the day that he makes, and he will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him.

l: day of the LORD's coming, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 3
s: The day of the LORD's coming is described as one that no one can easily endure or stand through, as he is like a refiner's fire and launderers' soap. On that day he purifies the sons of Levi, brings judgment on wrongdoers, and makes those who fear him his own possession.

l: The Book of Malachi, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 4
s: The LORD of Armies announces that the coming day will burn like a furnace, consuming the proud and all who work wickedness so that nothing remains of them, neither root nor branch. For those who fear his name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings, and they will leap like calves of the stall and tread down the wicked, who will become ashes under their feet. The LORD calls the people to remember the law of Moses his servant, given at Horeb for all Israel as statutes and ordinances. He promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes. Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers to children and children to fathers, so that the LORD does not come and strike the earth with a curse.

l: LORD of Armies, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 4
s: The LORD of Armies declares that the coming day will burn up the proud and the wicked, while the sun of righteousness will rise with healing for those who fear his name. He commands the people to remember the law of Moses his servant, given at Horeb. He promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day, so that he does not have to strike the earth with a curse.

l: day of the LORD's coming, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 4
s: The day is described as burning like a furnace and as coming to burn up the proud and all who work wickedness, leaving them neither root nor branch. It is called the day that the LORD makes, on which the wicked become ashes under the feet of the righteous. It is also named the great and terrible day of the LORD, and Elijah is to be sent before it comes.

l: proud and wicked people, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 4
s: The proud and all who work wickedness will become stubble, and the coming day will burn them up, leaving them neither root nor branch. They will be ashes under the soles of the feet of those who fear the LORD's name, who will tread them down.

l: those who fear the LORD's name, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 4
s: For those who fear the LORD's name, the sun of righteousness will arise with healing in its wings. They will go out and leap like calves of the stall, and they will tread down the wicked, who will be ashes under their feet in the day the LORD makes.

l: Elijah, The Book of Malachi, Chapter 4
s: Elijah the prophet is promised to be sent by the LORD before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest the LORD come and strike the earth with a curse.

This is the book of Genesis, fifty chapters moving from the creation of the world to the settling of one family in Egypt. God creates the heavens and earth in six days, makes man and woman in his image, and rests on the seventh. In Eden the serpent persuades the woman to eat the forbidden fruit, and the pair are expelled. Cain kills Abel, and genealogies run through Seth to Noah. As wickedness and violence grow, God sends a flood, saving Noah, his family and the animals in a ship. After the waters recede he makes a covenant with Noah, sealed by the rainbow. Noah's descendants spread into nations, and at Babel God confuses their language and scatters them. The focus then narrows to Abram, called by the LORD from Haran with promises of land, a great nation and blessing for all families. He is renamed Abraham, and Sarai becomes Sarah. Their story includes Lot's separation, the rescue of Lot, Melchizedek, the covenant of circumcision, Hagar and Ishmael, the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and the birth of Isaac. God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, then provides a ram instead. After Sarah dies and Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah, a servant finds Rebekah as Isaac's wife. Their twin sons Esau and Jacob quarrel. Esau sells his birthright, and Jacob, helped by Rebekah, obtains Isaac's blessing by deceit. Jacob flees to Laban, dreams at Bethel, marries Leah and Rachel, and fathers twelve sons and a daughter, Dinah. He grows rich, leaves Laban, wrestles with a man at the Jabbok and is renamed Israel. He is reconciled with Esau, but Dinah's violation leads Simeon and Levi to slaughter Shechem's men. Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and Isaac dies. Esau's line in Edom is listed. The last chapters centre on Joseph, Jacob's favored son. His brothers sell him into slavery, and in Egypt he is falsely accused by Potiphar's wife and jailed. After interpreting dreams for the cup bearer and baker, he interprets Pharaoh's dreams of seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and Pharaoh sets him over Egypt. Famine drives his brothers to buy grain. Joseph tests them, and Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place. Joseph then reveals himself, saying God sent him ahead to preserve life. Jacob and seventy of his house move to Goshen. Jacob blesses Ephraim and Manasseh and pronounces on his twelve sons, with Judah exalted. He dies and is buried at Machpelah. Joseph reassures his fearful brothers that God meant their act for good, and he dies in Egypt after making Israel's children swear to carry his bones out.

God is the central divine figure of these records, the creator and the sovereign actor behind events from the beginning of the world through the story of Jacob's family in Egypt. He is first shown creating the heavens and earth by speaking over six days, naming day, night, sky, earth and seas, dividing light from darkness, and making man in his image, then seeing all he made as very good. He forms Adam from dust, plants the Garden of Eden, makes a woman from the man's rib, and commands them not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. After the transgression he questions them, pronounces curses, clothes Adam and his wife in animal skins, and sends them out, placing cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life. He takes Enoch, who walked with him. Seeing the earth corrupt and violent, he tells Noah he will end all flesh, commands him to build a ship, and preserves his family and the creatures. After the flood he resolves not to curse the ground again, blesses Noah, and sets the rainbow as the sign of a covenant with every living creature. As God Almighty he then establishes an everlasting covenant with Abraham, changes the names of Abram and Sarai, commands circumcision, and promises Isaac through Sarah while also promising to bless Ishmael and make him a nation. He protects Sarah by warning Abimelech in a dream, tests Abraham over Isaac, and swears by himself to bless him and multiply his offspring. The promises pass to Isaac and to Jacob: land, countless offspring, blessing for all families, and his presence and protection. He opens Rachel's womb, appears at Bethel, renames Jacob Israel, and promises a nation and kings. He establishes Pharaoh's dream and, according to Joseph, sent Joseph ahead to Egypt to preserve life and save many alive, meaning for good what the brothers meant for evil. He tells Israel in a night vision to go down to Egypt, promising to make a great nation there and bring him up again. The records end with Joseph affirming that God will visit the Israelites and bring them out to the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

The heavens and the earth are an account of creation by God. It begins with a formless, empty, dark earth under God's Spirit, then is declared finished with its vast array. Before plants or man existed, a mist watered the ground; the LORD God formed man, trees, animals, and woman.

Earth begins formless, empty and water-covered; God gathers the waters into seas, revealing dry land called earth, which then yields grass, herbs and fruit trees, produces living creatures, and receives light from sky lights.
has_quality good God says "Let there be light," and light comes to be. God sees that it is good, divides it from the darkness, and calls it "day".
God makes an expanse in the middle of the waters to divide the waters above from the waters below, and calls it "sky". On the fourth day he sets lights in it, and on the fifth day birds fly in it.

has_quality good On the third day God commands the earth to yield grass, herbs yielding seed, and fruit trees, each after its kind, and it does so. God sees that they are good, and later gives them to man and to the animals as food.

Lights are celestial bodies God makes on the fourth day, along with the stars. Set in the sky's expanse, they give light to earth, mark seasons, days and years, and divide light from darkness; the greater rules day, the lesser night.
Sea creatures and birds are created by God on the fifth day, each after its kind, seen as good, then blessed and told to be fruitful, multiply, and fill the seas and earth.

made_by God [livestock, creeping things, animals of the earth] On the sixth day God has the earth produce livestock, creeping things, and animals of the earth, each after its kind, and he makes them. God sees that they are good, and gives every green herb to them for food.

Adam is the first man, made by God in his own likeness from dust of the ground, and the name also covers male and female together as created and blessed. God gives them dominion over land animals, fish and birds, and plants for food. Adam eats the fruit his wife gives him, hides from the LORD God, and blames the woman. As a result the ground is cursed, he must labor by the sweat of his face, and he is destined to return to dust. He gains knowledge of good and evil, is clothed in animal skins made by God, and is expelled from Eden to till the ground. He fathers Seth in his own likeness, has other sons and daughters, and dies at 930.

The world's creation unfolds over six days, each ending with evening and morning: light, sky, land and plants, sun, moon and stars, sea creatures and birds, then land animals and man; God judges it very good.

The man is a living soul formed from the dust of the ground and placed in the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it. Forbidden, on penalty of death, to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he names all livestock, birds and animals, finds no fitting helper among them, and receives the woman, made from his rib, as his wife.

Eve is the first woman, made by the LORD God from a rib taken from the man while he slept, and called 'woman' because she was taken out of Man. She is a helper comparable to him. She eats the fruit she finds desirable, gives some to her husband, and blames the serpent's deceit. She is told her pain in childbirth will be multiplied and her husband will rule over her. The man names her Eve as mother of all the living. She later bears Cain, Abel, and Seth, the last given in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.

The Garden of Eden is a place planted by the LORD God eastward in Eden, filled with pleasant, food-bearing trees, including the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in its middle. A river flowing out of Eden waters it and divides into four rivers. The man is placed there to cultivate and keep it. It later becomes the setting of the serpent's temptation and the couple's hiding. The man is sent out, and cherubim with a flaming sword guard its east against access to the tree of life.

l: tree of the knowledge of good and evil, Genesis
s: The tree of the knowledge of good and evil stands in the middle of the garden beside the tree of life, made by the LORD God. He forbids eating or touching its fruit on pain of death. The woman sees it as good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable for wisdom. After the serpent claims it will open their eyes, she eats and gives to the man. God then confirms the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.
The seventh day is when God finished his creation work and rested, then blessed the day and made it holy because he rested in it.

The serpent is an animal of the field made by the LORD God, noted as more subtle than any other. In Chapter 3 it questions the woman about God's command, tells her she won't die and will become like God, and she says it deceived her. The LORD God then curses it above all livestock and animals: it must go on its belly and eat dust, with hostility set between its offspring and the woman's.

l: eating the forbidden fruit (the Fall), Genesis
s: The Fall: persuaded by the serpent, the woman eats the fruit first and gives some to her husband Adam, who eats. Their eyes open to their nakedness; they sew fig leaves and hide, then God questions them, pronounces curses, and expels the man from the garden.

A set of curses and punishments in Chapter 3. The serpent is cursed to go on its belly and eat dust, with hostility between offspring. The woman receives multiplied childbirth pain and her husband's rule. Adam faces cursed ground with thorns and thistles, sweat-earned bread, return to dust, and expulsion from the garden away from the tree of life.

Cain, a tiller of the ground and brother of Abel, offers a sacrifice the LORD does not respect, grows angry, and kills Abel. Cursed as a fugitive and wanderer yet given a protective sign, he settles in Nod east of Eden, fathers Enoch, builds a city, and founds Lamech's line.
Abel, Cain's brother, is a sheep keeper who offers the firstborn of his flock and is favored by the LORD; Cain kills him in the field, his blood cries out, and Seth replaces him.

The LORD is the divine figure who acts throughout these records, treated here as a single entity though it is not a human person. He is described as possessor of heaven and earth, God Most High, God of Abraham, a God who sees (a name given by Hagar), and Judge of all the earth. The records begin with him respecting Abel's offering but not Cain's, confronting and cursing Cain, and promising sevenfold vengeance on anyone who kills him. He then grieves over human wickedness, limits man's days to one hundred twenty years, and resolves to destroy life. Noah finds favor, and the LORD commands him to enter the ship with his household, sends forty days and nights of rain, and shuts him in. At Babel he confuses the language of the people and scatters them across the earth. The central thread is his relationship with Abram/Abraham. He calls Abram, promises a great nation, blessing for the families of the earth, and the land of Canaan to his offspring forever, with offspring as countless as the dust and the stars. He calls himself Abram's shield and exceedingly great reward, reminds him that he brought him out of Ur, and makes a covenant, foretelling the servitude of Abram's offspring and judgment on the nation they serve. He afflicts Pharaoh over Sarai, hears Hagar's affliction, and asks 'Is anything too hard for the LORD?' while promising Sarah a son. He agrees to spare Sodom for ten righteous but rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, showing mercy to Lot. The promises pass on: Abraham's servant invokes him, and he appears to Isaac, reaffirming the oath sworn to Abraham and blessing Isaac's harvest and flocks. He opens Leah's womb when she is hated, and Leah credits him with seeing her affliction. The records end with him being with Joseph in Potiphar's house and in prison, making all that Joseph does prosper and blessing Potiphar's house for Joseph's sake. Overall he moves from judge and destroyer to covenant-making promiser and faithful protector of chosen people.
Seth, Adam's son in his likeness, fathered Enosh at 105, had more children over 807 years, and died aged 912.
Enosh, son of Seth, fathered Kenan at 90, had other sons and daughters over 815 more years, and died at 905.

Lamech is a man appearing in two chapters. In the first, a descendant of Cain, he takes wives Adah and Zillah, fathers several children, and boasts of slaying a young man, claiming seventy-seven-fold vengeance. In the second, born to Methuselah, he fathers Noah at 182, hopes he will bring comfort from cursed toil, and dies at 777.
desire_for Cain [to be ruled over by him] The LORD tells Cain that sin crouches at the door, that its desire is for him, and that he is to rule over it. Cain then kills Abel.

perpetrator Cain Cain invites Abel into the field, rises up against him, and kills him. The LORD confronts Cain, says Abel's blood cries from the ground, and curses Cain to be a fugitive and wanderer, though he also appoints a sign to protect him.
Kenan, son of Enosh, fathered Mahalalel at 70, had other sons and daughters over 840 more years, and died at 910.
Mahalalel, son of Kenan, fathered Jared at 65, had more children over 830 years, and died aged 895.
Jared, son of Mahalalel, fathered Enoch at 162, lived 800 more years having other children, and died at 962.
Enoch, son of Jared, fathered Methuselah at 65, then walked with God 300 years and had more children; at 365 years he did not die but was taken by God.
Methuselah, born to Enoch, fathered Lamech at 187, had other children for 782 more years, and died at 969.

Noah is a righteous, blameless man who walks with God and finds favor with the LORD. Born to Lamech, who named him in hope of comfort from the toil of the cursed ground, he becomes father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth at age 500. Because of his righteousness, God commands him to build a ship, and he does everything he is told. At age six hundred he enters the ship with his family and the animals, and the LORD shuts him in. The flood destroys all other life, leaving only those aboard. Afterward Noah sends out a raven and a dove, learning the waters have abated when the dove returns with an olive leaf. He leaves the ship at God's command, builds an altar to the LORD, and offers burnt offerings of clean animals and birds. God blesses him and establishes a covenant with him, his sons, and his descendants. Noah then becomes a farmer and plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered in his tent, and on waking curses Canaan, blesses the God of Shem, and asks that Japheth be enlarged. He lives 350 years after the flood and dies at 950. His sons' families become the nations that divided.

Shem is one of Noah's three sons and elder brother of Japheth. He leaves the ship, helps cover his father's nakedness while walking backwards, and receives Noah's blessing of the LORD as his God. He fathers Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad (at age 100), Lud and Aram, and is father of all Eber's children, with descendants listed.

Ham is one of Noah's three sons and father of Canaan. He sees his father's nakedness and tells his brothers, and Noah learns what his youngest son did. Later, his sons Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan are listed, with descendants traced and the Canaanite border described.

Japheth is one of Noah's three sons. He and Shem cover their father with a garment, and Noah blesses him to be enlarged, dwell in Shem's tents, and have Canaan as servant. He fathers seven sons, including Gomer and Javan, whose descendants divide the islands of the nations by language, family and nation.

is_a book The chapter opens by calling itself the book of the generations of Adam. It records the line from Adam to Noah's sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, with each man's age at his heir's birth, years afterward, and total lifespan.
Men multiplied and took wives; their hearts grew continually and only evil, so the LORD resolved to destroy them, limiting their lifespan to one hundred twenty years because they are flesh.

The flood is a catastrophic deluge brought by God to destroy all flesh having the breath of life, sparing only those kept alive in the ship. God announces it first. It begins on the seventeenth day of the second month of Noah's six hundredth year, when the deep's fountains burst open and the sky's windows open. Rain falls forty days and nights, and the waters rise fifteen cubits above the high mountains, covering the whole earth and killing all life on dry land. Waters flood the earth for one hundred fifty days. God then sends a wind, stops the fountains and windows, and the waters recede, showing mountain tops in the tenth month. They are dried up by the first day of the first month of Noah's 601st year, and the earth is dry by the twenty-seventh day of the second month. God afterward promises it will never happen again.

Noah's ship is a vessel God commanded him to build from gopher wood, sealed with pitch, three hundred cubits long, with a side door, a roof, and three levels. Noah, his household, and pairs of animals and birds enter, and the LORD shuts them in. As waters rise, it floats, carrying the only survivors. It rests on Ararat on the seventeenth day of the seventh month. Noah opens its window, removes its covering, and all aboard leave at God's command.

l: covenant (God's covenant with Noah, his offspring, and every living creature), Genesis
s: God establishes his covenant with Noah, his offspring, and every living creature that left the ship, promising that all flesh will never again be cut off by the waters of a flood. He calls it an everlasting covenant for perpetual generations, with the rainbow as its token.
The earth, corrupted before God and filled with wickedness and violence by all flesh, is condemned: God resolves to destroy it and all flesh with a flood.

The LORD first resolved to destroy animals, creeping things, and birds along with man. God then told Noah to bring two of every sort, male and female, of birds, livestock, and creeping things into the ship to keep them alive, along with food for them.

The LORD saw that man's wickedness was great and that every thought of his heart was continually only evil. The earth was corrupt and filled with violence, which became the reason God resolved to bring an end to all flesh.

l: Noah's family (Noah's wife, sons and sons' wives), Genesis
s: Noah's household (wife, sons Shem, Ham, Japheth, and their three wives) is commanded by the LORD to enter the ship with Noah on the same day, is shut in by the LORD, and survives the flood with him.

is_located_in ship (Noah's ship) God remembers the animals and livestock along with Noah in the ship. At God's command every animal, creeping thing, and bird goes out of the ship after their families, so that they may breed abundantly, be fruitful, and multiply on the earth. Clean animals and birds are taken by Noah for burnt offerings.

Clean and unclean animals, birds, livestock, and creeping things go into the ship by pairs, male and female, after their kinds, as God commanded; seven pairs of clean animals and of birds are to be taken to keep seed alive. All flesh on the earth and dry land that had the breath of life, including every man, dies in the flood. Only those in the ship with Noah are left.

A female dove sent out by Noah to test whether the waters have abated: first finding no rest and returning, then returning a week later with a fresh olive leaf, and after another week, sent again, she does not return.
A group of Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, who are the source of Chapter 10's genealogy; their descendants are listed in turn, and the nations divided from them after the flood.

has_state dry [second month, twenty-seventh day] The earth is covered by waters at first, then emerges as a wind passes over it, with the mountain tops visible in the tenth month and the ground dry by the second month of the following year. The living creatures from the ship go out onto it to breed and multiply. God declares that while the earth remains, seed time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, and day and night will not cease.

l: God's promise not to curse the ground again, Genesis
s: After smelling Noah's pleasing offerings, the LORD resolves in his heart not to curse the ground again nor strike every living thing, despite man's heart being evil from youth. He adds that seed time, harvest, cold, heat, summer, winter, day and night will continue while earth remains.

Canaan, son of Ham, is cursed by Noah to be a servant of servants, specifically to Shem and Japheth. He fathers Sidon (firstborn) and Heth, and his descendants include the Jebusites, Amorites, Hivites, and other peoples.

God sets his rainbow in the cloud as the sign of the covenant between him and the earth. When it appears in the cloud, God says he will look at it and remember the everlasting covenant with every living creature.

Nimrod, son of Cush, began to be a mighty one on the earth and was a mighty hunter before the LORD, giving rise to a saying. His kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in Shinar; he then went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth Ir, Calah and Resen.

is_named_for confusion of language [LORD confused the language there] Babel is the name given to the city the people were building, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. From there the LORD scattered the people over the whole earth.
Philistines, descended from Casluhim and ruled by king Abimelech, envy Isaac's wealth; having earlier filled Abraham's wells with earth, their Gerar herdsmen now quarrel with Isaac's over water.

Sodom is a city of the plain in the valley of Siddim, whose inhabitants are described as exceedingly wicked sinners against the LORD. Lot moves his tent there. Its king, with other kings, rebelled against Chedorlaomer and was defeated; its goods were taken and Lot carried off, until Abram recovered them. Later the cry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin grievous, and the LORD agrees to spare it for as few as ten righteous. Its men surround Lot's house demanding to have sex with his guests. The angels announce the outcry has grown too great, and Sodom is overthrown with sulfur and fire from the sky, along with Gomorrah, the plain, and all inhabitants.
Shelah is Judah's third son, born at Chezib, and father of Eber. Though grown, Judah withholds him from Tamar as husband, fearing he will die like his brothers, and later admits it.

occurs_after flood The division is described as the islands of the nations being divided in their lands by language, family, and nation, and each line of Japheth, Ham, and Shem is closed with similar wording. Peleg, a son of Eber, was named for the earth being divided in his days, and the chapter ends stating that the nations divided from Noah's sons' families after the flood.

l: people of the earth (builders of Babel), Genesis
s: The people of the earth share one language, settle on a plain in Shinar, and use bricks and tar to build a city and tower at Babel to make a name and avoid scattering. The LORD confuses their language, scatters them, and building stops.

has_height top reaches to the sky [intended] The people plan the tower with its top reaching to the sky, built of burnt brick with tar for mortar, alongside the city. The LORD comes down to see it, and the building is stopped when he confuses their language and scatters them.

l: language of all the earth, Genesis
s: At the start of the chapter the whole earth has one language and one speech. The LORD confuses it so people cannot understand one another's speech, which leads to their scattering.

Terah, descendant of Nahor in Shem's line, lived 205 years and fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran. After Haran died in Ur, he led Abram, Lot, and Sarai toward Canaan, settled in Haran instead, and died there.

Abraham, first called Abram, is a man described as a Hebrew, originating from Ur of the Chaldees, son of Terah, brother of Nahor and Haran, and uncle of Lot. He is married to Sarai, later called Sarah. The records follow him from his origins to his death at 175, buried with Sarah in the cave of Machpelah. What matters most is his relationship with the LORD: he obeys, worships, builds altars, receives promises of land, countless offspring and a covenant, and is credited with righteousness for believing. He is called a prophet, a servant of the LORD, and a prince of God, and his obedience is later named as the reason for promises to Isaac. The story begins with his journey from Ur toward Canaan, stopping at Haran. At seventy-five he leaves Haran with Sarai and Lot, building altars through Canaan. In famine he goes to Egypt and, fearing for his life, has Sarai say she is his sister; he gains wealth, is rebuked and sent away. Returning very rich, he separates from Lot, offering first choice of land, and settles by the oaks of Mamre in Hebron. With 318 trained men and his allies Mamre, Eshcol and Aner, he rescues Lot, gives Melchizedek a tenth, and refuses the king of Sodom's goods. Childless, with Eliezer as presumptive heir, he is promised an heir of his own body. At eighty-six Ishmael is born to Hagar. At ninety-nine God renames him Abraham, promises he will be father of nations, and he circumcises his household. He shows hospitality to three visitors, pleads for Sodom, and sees its smoke; God remembers him and rescues Lot. In Gerar he repeats the sister claim to Abimelech, and God heals Abimelech's household through his prayer. At one hundred Isaac is born; he sends Hagar and Ishmael away, makes a covenant with Abimelech over a well at Beersheba, and calls on the Everlasting God. He obeys the command to offer Isaac, is stopped, sacrifices a ram, and names the place The LORD Will Provide. After mourning Sarah he buys Ephron's field and cave as a burial place, then sends his servant to find Isaac a wife from his relatives. He takes Keturah, fathers six more sons, gives all he has to Isaac, and dies full of years.

Lot is a man, the grandson of Terah through Haran, who dies in Ur while Terah lives. Terah takes Lot toward Canaan, and they settle in Haran. Lot later travels with Abram, owning his own flocks, herds, and tents. When offered a choice of land, he picks the well-watered Plain of the Jordan, separates from Abram, and moves his tent as far as Sodom, where he lives as a foreigner. Four kings capture him with his goods, and Abram rescues him. In Sodom he sits in the gate, hosts two angels, and offers his virgin daughters to the crowd to protect them. Pulled inside by the angels, he lingers, is led out by the hand, and pleads to go to Zoar. He then lives in a cave in the mountain with his daughters, God having remembered Abraham and saved him. There his daughters get him drunk and lie with him, making him father of Moab and Ben Ammi.

Sarah, first called Sarai, is the beautiful wife and half-sister of Abram/Abraham (daughter of his father, not his mother). The records open with her barrenness and childlessness as she travels with Terah, Abram and Lot from Ur toward Canaan and settles in Haran. In Egypt, Abram has her say she is his sister; Pharaoh takes her, plagues follow, and she is returned. Still childless, she gives her servant Hagar to Abram, then deals harshly with Hagar after being despised, and Hagar flees. God renames her Sarah, promises to bless her and give Abraham a son by her, and says she will be a mother of nations with kings descending from her. At ninety, old and past childbearing, she overhears the promise at the tent door, laughs, then denies it out of fear. Abimelech takes her after Abraham again calls her his sister, but does not approach her and restores her, declaring her vindicated. She conceives and bears Isaac in Abraham's old age as God had spoken, says God has made her laugh, and later, seeing Hagar's son mocking, asks Abraham to cast out Hagar and her son so he will not share Isaac's inheritance. Sarah lives 127 years and dies at Kiriath Arba (Hebron) in Canaan. Abraham mourns her and buries her in the cave of Machpelah, Ephron's field before Mamre.

Canaan is a land inhabited by Canaanites and Perizzites. Abram, Sarai, and Lot enter it, and Abram travels through Shechem, Bethel, and toward the South. After Lot departs, the LORD promises Abram and his offspring all the land he sees. Later, famine strikes Canaan, afflicting Jacob's family and sending the brothers to buy food. Finally, the brothers return with Pharaoh's wagons and provisions, telling Jacob that Joseph is alive, and Jacob resolves to go see him.

Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, who rules the land and has servants and officers, including a chief cup bearer and chief baker. He ranks above Joseph only in the throne. Early on he takes Sarai into his house, deals well with Abram for her sake, then suffers plagues sent by the LORD, rebukes Abram, and sends him away with an escort. Later he imprisons his cup bearer and baker in anger, then on his birthday restores the cup bearer and hangs the baker. Troubled by two dreams that no magician or wise man can interpret, he summons Joseph, accepts his interpretation, and sets him over Egypt with a signet ring, linen robes, gold chain, new name, and wife Asenath. In the famine he directs Egyptians to Joseph. Pleased that Joseph's brothers have come, he sends wagons for Jacob's family and promises them the good of the land. He grants them Goshen, asks Jacob his age, and is blessed by him. Through Joseph's actions he owns all Egypt's land except the priests' and receives a fifth of harvests. Finally he lets Joseph go bury his father.

The Egyptians are a people portrayed first as a perceived threat to Abram, who fears they will kill him for Sarai's beauty, which Pharaoh's princes praise. Later, in famine, they trade money, livestock, bodies and land for bread and seed, are moved to cities by Joseph, give Pharaoh a fifth, and become his servants. They avoid eating with Hebrews.

Egypt is a land ruled by Pharaoh, described as good and fat, with grain available for purchase and a region called Goshen. Its people regard shepherds as an abomination. It first appears as a refuge: Abram lives there as a foreigner during a severe famine, Sarai is taken into Pharaoh's house, which is plagued, and Abram is sent away with his wife and possessions. Later Joseph is brought there by merchants and sold to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. After Pharaoh's magicians fail to interpret his dreams, Joseph is set over the whole land. It produces abundantly for seven years, stores food, then endures famine yet has bread, and people from all countries come to buy. Jacob sends his sons to buy grain; Joseph rules and reveals himself. Pharaoh offers the best land, and Jacob's household of seventy comes, settling in Goshen. As famine continues, all land except the priests' becomes Pharaoh's, with a fifth owed to him, and Jacob's family multiplies exceedingly.

Bethel is a place in Canaan, formerly the city Luz, west of Abram's tent with Ai to the east. Jacob names it after sleeping and dreaming there, calling it God's house and the gate of heaven. Later God speaks with Jacob there again; he builds an altar, calls it El Beth El, sets up a stone pillar, and Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, is buried below it.
has_severity severe [in the land] A severe famine strikes the land and causes Abram to go down into Egypt to live as a foreigner. It sets in motion the episode involving Sarai and Pharaoh.

l: promise of the land and blessing, Genesis
s: The LORD promises Abram a great nation, a great name, blessing for those who bless him and a curse for those who treat him with contempt, and blessing for all the families of the earth through him. At Shechem he also promises to give the land to Abram's offspring, and Abram builds an altar in response.

Abram's offspring are a promised line descending from his own body, central to a covenant. Early promises give them the land forever and numbers like the dust and stars. Then they are told they will live as foreigners in a land not theirs, serving and afflicted four hundred years, before leaving with great wealth after that nation is judged, returning in the fourth generation. Finally the covenant becomes everlasting: God will be their God, Canaan their possession, males circumcised, nations and kings arising, the line running through Isaac, and they will bless the nations.

l: strife between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen, Genesis
s: Strife between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen erupts because the land cannot support both men's great livestock and possessions together, with Canaanites and Perizzites present. Abram cites it as his reason to propose separating, and the separation follows.

The Plain of the Jordan is a region Lot surveys and finds well-watered everywhere, resembling the garden of the LORD and Egypt toward Zoar, before Sodom and Gomorrah's destruction. Lot chooses it for himself, and its cities become his home.
Zoar is a small nearby city, named a 'little one' by Lot, whom he asks to flee to instead of the mountains. The angel spares it; Lot arrives at sunrise but later leaves, afraid to live there.

Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, was served twelve years by five kings who rebelled in the thirteenth. Allied with Amraphel, he struck several peoples in the fourteenth year and defeated the five kings at Siddim, but was afterward slaughtered by Abram's pursuit.

Bera, king of Sodom, fought in the valley of Siddim and fled when tar pits took his men. After Abram's victory he asked Abram to return the people and keep the goods; Abram refused anything beyond what was eaten and his allies' share.
Melchizedek is king of Salem and priest of God Most High; after Abram's victory he brings bread and wine, blesses Abram in God's name, and receives a tenth of all from him.

inhabits Seir (hill country) [inhabitants of the land] The Horites are the sons of Seir, inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan, whose children and chiefs are listed. Their chiefs are named in the land of Seir and in the land of Edom, and Anah is noted for finding the hot springs in the wilderness while feeding his father Zibeon's donkeys.

Esau settled in the hill country of Seir after leaving Canaan and his brother Jacob. It is described as the land of the Horites, the children of Seir, who were its inhabitants, and Esau is called the father of the Edomites there.

l: war of the four kings against the five, Genesis
s: A battle in the valley of Siddim where four kings, including Chedorlaomer, fought five kings who rebelled after thirteen years of service. The five fled, some falling into tar pits; the victors seized goods and food and captured Lot, until Abram's night pursuit recovered captives and goods.

The land is the territory promised to Abram's offspring, stretching from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates and inhabited by ten peoples, including Hittites, Amorites and Canaanites. Possession is delayed until the fourth generation, since the Amorite's iniquity is not yet full.

A covenant the LORD makes with Abram concerning the promised land. After animals are divided and Abram sleeps, a smoking furnace and flaming torch pass between the pieces, and the land from Egypt's river to the Euphrates is given to his offspring.

Hagar is an Egyptian servant of Sarai (Sarah) and Abraham, given to Abram as a wife. Pregnant, she looks down on Sarai, is treated harshly, and flees; the LORD's angel meets her by a fountain, sends her back, and promises many offspring. She bears Ishmael. Later Abraham sends her and her child away; in the wilderness of Beersheba, as water runs out, God's angel reassures her and God shows her a well. She gets her son an Egyptian wife.

Ishmael is the son of Abram (Abraham) and Hagar, announced by the LORD's angel before birth and foretold as a wild donkey among men, opposed to all his brothers. Born when Abram was eighty-six, he is circumcised at thirteen. God keeps the covenant for Isaac but blesses Ishmael, promising fruitfulness, twelve princes and a great nation. After Sarah sees him mocking, he is sent away with Hagar; God hears him in the wilderness and provides water. He grows up as an archer in the wilderness of Paran and marries a woman from Egypt, obtained by Hagar. He helps Isaac bury Abraham, fathers twelve sons beginning with Nebaioth and Kedar, who become princes of their nations, and dies at 137, gathered to his people.

Isaac is the long-awaited son of Abraham and Sarah, named at God's direction before his birth, with God promising an everlasting covenant with him and his offspring. He is born at the set time, circumcised on the eighth day, and weaned amid a great feast. Called Abraham's only, beloved son, he is commanded to be offered as a burnt offering; he carries the wood, asks about the lamb, and is bound on the altar, but is spared when the angel intervenes and a ram is offered instead. A wife is sought for him from Abraham's homeland's kin rather than taking him back there; he meets Rebekah, brings her into his mother Sarah's tent, loves her, and is comforted after Sarah's death. He inherits all Abraham had, and after Abraham's death God blesses him and he lives by Beer Lahai Roi. Married at forty, he entreats the LORD for barren Rebekah, and at sixty twins Esau and Jacob are born. He favors Esau because he ate his venison. During a famine he goes to Gerar, is told not to go to Egypt, and out of fear claims Rebekah is his sister. He sows and reaps a hundredfold, becomes very great, is sent away by Abimelech, reopens his father's wells, digs new ones, and settles at Beersheba, where he builds an altar and makes a covenant with Abimelech. Old and blind, he tries to bless Esau but is deceived into blessing Jacob; he trembles, affirms the blessing, and gives Esau a lesser one of living by the sword and serving his brother. He then blesses Jacob again, forbids a Canaanite wife, sends him to Laban's daughters in Paddan Aram, and wishes him the blessing of Abraham. His displeasure with Canaanite daughters prompts Esau's new marriage. At Mamre (Kiriath Arba, Hebron), Jacob comes to him. Isaac dies at 180, old and full of days, and is buried by Esau and Jacob.

God declares his covenant with Abraham and his offspring to be everlasting, promising to multiply Abraham, make him father of nations with kings among them, be their God, and give them all the land of Canaan. Abraham and his offspring are to keep it, and it is to be in their flesh. God says it will be established specifically with Isaac, and that anyone uncircumcised has broken it.

God commands that every male be circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin as a token of the covenant, at eight days old, including those born in the house or bought from foreigners. An uncircumcised male is to be cut off from his people for breaking the covenant. Abraham, aged ninety-nine, and Ishmael, aged thirteen, are circumcised on the same day along with all the men of the house.

Every male in Abraham's household, whether born in the house or bought with money from a foreigner, is included in the circumcision command even if not of his offspring. Abraham circumcises all of them on the same day as God had said. All the men of his house are circumcised with him.

travels_toward Sodom Three men stand near Abraham as he sits at his tent door. He bows, washes-their-feet hospitality is offered, and they eat and agree to stay. They ask about Sarah, announce that she will have a son, then rise and look toward Sodom. Two of them go toward Sodom while Abraham remains before the LORD.

Abraham asks whether the LORD will consume the righteous with the wicked. The LORD agrees to spare the whole place for fifty, then forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and finally ten righteous found within it. The text does not say whether any are found.

has_cause fear [reason for her denial] Sarah laughs within herself, wondering whether she will have pleasure now that she and her lord are old. The LORD repeats her words to Abraham and asks why she laughed. She denies it, afraid, and is told that she did laugh.

concerns Sodom [pleading to spare it for the righteous] Abraham comes near and appeals to the Judge of all the earth to do right and not kill the righteous with the wicked. He acknowledges he is dust and ashes and lowers the number step by step from fifty to ten, twice asking that the Lord not be angry. The LORD grants each request, then goes his way, and Abraham returns to his place.

l: destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Genesis
s: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah is the LORD's overthrow of the cities and the whole plain. It is first only considered, with a promise to spare the city for ten righteous. After the outcry grows great and Lot reaches Zoar, the LORD rains sulfur and fire, destroying everything, and Abraham sees smoke rising next morning.

is_promised_to Sarah [to be born at the set time next year] The visitors say that Sarah will have a son at about this time next year. The LORD repeats the promise after Sarah laughs, saying that at the set time, when the season comes around, Sarah will have a son. The narrator notes that Abraham and Sarah are old and she is past the age of childbearing.

is_sent_by the LORD [to destroy Sodom] The two angels come to Sodom at evening, at first say they will stay in the street, then go home with Lot and eat his feast. They pull Lot inside, strike the crowd with blindness, and announce that they are sent to destroy the city. They hurry Lot, his wife, and his daughters out by the hand, set them outside the city, and agree to spare Zoar.

inhabit Sodom [young and old, from every quarter] The men of Sodom, young and old from every quarter, surround Lot's house and demand that he bring out his guests so they can have sex with them. They reject Lot's offer of his daughters, call him a foreigner who appoints himself judge, threaten to deal worse with him, and press to break the door. The angels strike them with blindness so that they weary themselves trying to find the door.

becomes pillar of salt [after looking back] Lot's wife is taken by the hand and led out of Sodom by the angels along with Lot and their two daughters. She looks back from behind him and becomes a pillar of salt.

commit incest of Lot's daughters with Lot [to preserve family line] Lot's two virgin daughters are offered by Lot to the men of Sodom, who do not take them. They are led out of the city with their parents and live with Lot in a cave in the mountain. Both become pregnant by their father and bear sons.

is_mother_of Moab The firstborn proposes to her younger sister that they make their father drink wine and lie with him to preserve the family line, since no man is left to come in to them. She lies with Lot the first night and bears a son named Moab.
is_mother_of Ben Ammi The younger daughter is urged by her sister to join the plan and lies with Lot the second night after they make him drink wine. She bears a son named Ben Ammi.
is_father_of Moabites Moab is the son born to Lot's firstborn daughter by her father. He is named as the father of the Moabites to this day.
is_father_of Ammonites (children of Ammon) Ben Ammi is the son born to Lot's younger daughter by her father. He is named as the father of the children of Ammon to this day.

l: incest of Lot's daughters with Lot, Genesis
s: has_motive preserving family line [no man available] Believing no man is left on earth to come in to them, Lot's daughters plan to preserve their father's family line. On two successive nights they make him drink wine, and first the firstborn and then the younger lies with him, without his knowing when they lie down or rise. Both become pregnant and bear Moab and Ben Ammi.

Abimelech is the king of Gerar, with Phicol as his army captain. He takes Sarah, is warned by God in a dream, and pleads the integrity of his heart. He restores her, rebukes Abraham, and gives him livestock, servants, and silver. After Abraham prays, God heals his household. Later he and Phicol seek Abraham's oath, and they make a covenant before he returns to the Philistines' land.
Gerar is where Isaac goes to Abimelech during the famine and lives for a long time. He later moves to the valley of Gerar, where his servants find a well and its herdsmen contend with his.

The sister claim is Abraham's statement that Sarah is his sister, echoed by Sarah at his request. It is true only in part, as she is his father's daughter, not his mother's. It leads Abimelech to take her; after Abraham explains his fear, Sarah is restored and Abraham enriched.

Beersheba is a wilderness place named for an oath sworn there by Abraham and Abimelech, who made a covenant. Abraham plants a tamarisk and calls on the LORD; Hagar wanders there. Later Isaac, visited by the LORD, builds an altar and digs a well called Shibah, giving the city its name.
Abraham complains that Abimelech's servants violently took away a water well. Abimelech says he knew nothing of it, and Abraham gives seven ewe lambs as a witness that he dug this well.
serves_as witness [that Abraham dug the well] Abraham sets seven ewe lambs of the flock apart by themselves. He tells Abimelech to take them from his hand as a witness that Abraham dug the well.

After Abimelech asks for an oath of fair dealing, Abraham agrees to swear, gives sheep and cattle to Abimelech, and the two make a covenant. It is made at Beersheba, which is named for the oath both swore there.

is_a messenger of the LORD [speaks from the sky] The LORD's angel calls to Abraham from the sky, telling him not to lay a hand on the boy, because God now knows that Abraham fears him. He calls a second time, speaking the LORD's oath that Abraham will be blessed, his offspring multiplied, and all nations blessed through his offspring because he obeyed.

God commands that Isaac be offered as a burnt offering on a mountain in Moriah, and Abraham brings the wood, fire, and knife for it. When Isaac asks where the lamb is, Abraham says God will provide it. Abraham finally offers a ram as the burnt offering instead of his son.
A ram caught by its horns in a thicket appears after the angel stops Abraham; he offers it as a burnt offering instead of Isaac and names the place "The LORD Will Provide."

Rebekah is the very beautiful daughter of Bethuel and sister of Laban. She draws water for a servant and his camels, receives gifts, is blessed by her family, agrees to go, and veils herself on seeing Isaac, becoming his wife. Initially barren, she conceives after Isaac entreats the LORD; told two nations are in her womb and the elder will serve the younger, she bears twins, Esau and Jacob, and loves Jacob. Isaac calls her his sister out of fear until Abimelech sees them. She and Isaac grieve over Esau's Hittite wives. She engineers Jacob's blessing by cooking goats and disguising him, then sends him to Laban to escape Esau, telling Isaac she is weary of life because of the daughters of Heth.
At Moriah, God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer his only son Isaac as a burnt offering; Abraham obeys fully until an angel stops him, then an oath of blessing follows.

Ephron the Hittite, son of Zohar and member of the children of Heth, owned the cave of Machpelah. He first offered it freely, then, as Abraham insisted on paying, named four hundred shekels of silver and received it.

The children of Heth received Abraham's request, called him a prince of God among them, and offered him the best of their tombs. Abraham bowed to them and asked them to entreat Ephron; they witnessed the sale at the city gate, and the field and cave were deeded to Abraham in their presence.

The cave of Machpelah is a burial site in Ephron the Hittite's field, before Mamre (Hebron) in Canaan. Abraham bought it with the field from Ephron as a burial possession. Sarah was buried there first; later Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, and Leah were too, and Jacob named it as his own desired burial place.

located_in field (Ephron's field) [at the end of the field] Abraham asked that Ephron sell him the cave of Machpelah, which lay in the end of Ephron's field. It was deeded to Abraham along with the field, and Sarah was buried in it.
Ephron's field at Machpelah, before Mamre, holds a cave and trees within its borders; offered as a gift, Abraham paid for it and it was deeded to him before the children of Heth.

is_possession_of Abraham Abraham asked the children of Heth for a possession of a burying-place so he could bury his dead out of his sight. He obtained it when the field and cave were deeded to him as a possession for a burial place, and Sarah was buried there.

l: silver purchase (Abraham's payment for the field), Genesis
s: Abraham pays Ephron the son of Zohar 400 shekels of silver, weighed out by the current merchants' standard, for the land; Ephron names the price, Abraham pays before the children of Heth, and field, cave, and trees are deeded at the city gate.

Abraham's servant swears the oath, travels to the city of Nahor with ten camels, and prays at the spring for a sign, which Rebekah fulfills. He gives her gold gifts, worships the LORD, tells her family his story, secures their consent, gives gifts to Rebekah and her family, and brings her to Isaac, to whom he reports all he had done.

Laban is a Syrian man of Haran, son of Bethuel and Nahor's line, brother of Rebekah, and thus Jacob's mother's brother. He fathers Rachel and Leah, owns flocks and household gods (teraphim), and invokes the God of Abraham and Nahor. In Chapter 24 he runs to the spring at the sight of the ring and bracelets, welcomes Abraham's servant, and with Bethuel says the matter is from the LORD and lets Rebekah go. In Chapter 29 he welcomes Jacob as his bone and flesh, offers wages, deceives him by giving Leah instead of Rachel, and secures seven more years of service. In Chapter 30 he asks Jacob to stay, having divined that the LORD blessed him for Jacob's sake, agrees to Jacob's wages, then removes the marked animals to his sons, setting three days' distance between them. In Chapter 31 his favor turns; he pursues the fleeing Jacob seven days to Gilead, is warned by God in a dream, accuses Jacob of stealing his gods, finds nothing, proposes a covenant, blesses his children, and returns home.

l: spring (outside the city of Nahor), Genesis
s: The spring outside the city of Nahor is where the servant makes his camels kneel at evening, when women come to draw water, and where he prays for a sign. Rebekah draws water there for him and his camels, and Laban comes out to meet the man there.

Abraham makes his servant swear by the LORD, with his hand under Abraham's thigh, not to take a Canaanite wife for Isaac but to find one among Abraham's relatives. The oath releases the servant if the woman is unwilling, though he must not bring Isaac back; the servant repeats its terms to Rebekah's family.

home_of Laban [destination of Jacob] Paddan Aram is the destination to which Isaac sends Jacob, to the house of Bethuel, Rebekah's father, to take a wife from the daughters of Laban. Laban is described as son of Bethuel the Syrian and brother of Rebekah. Jacob sets out toward it from Beersheba, heading toward Haran.

Esau is the elder twin son of Isaac and Rebekah, born red and hairy, who grows into a skillful hunter and man of the field favored by Isaac. Famished, he trades his birthright to his brother Jacob for red stew and lentils, earning the name Edom, and the text says he despised the birthright. When Jacob takes Isaac's blessing, Esau weeps and receives a lesser one of fertile dwelling, living by the sword, and serving his brother. He then hates Jacob and resolves to kill him after Isaac's death. Seeing that Canaanite women displease his father, he marries Mahalath, Ishmael's daughter, in addition to his other wives. Later, living in Seir, the land of Edom, he approaches Jacob with four hundred men, terrifying him. Yet Esau runs to meet him, embraces, kisses, and weeps, says he has enough, and accepts Jacob's gift only after urging, then returns toward Seir. His wives Adah, Oholibamah, and Basemath bear Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. Because their possessions are too great to share a dwelling with Jacob's, he moves his household and livestock to the hill country of Seir. He is identified as Edom and as father of the Edomites.

Jacob is a man, the younger twin son of Isaac and Rebekah, born holding his brother Esau's heel, which gives him his name. A quiet, smooth-skinned man who lives in tents, he buys Esau's birthright for bread and lentil stew and then obtains Isaac's blessing by deceit, wearing Esau's clothes and goat skins at Rebekah's urging. Esau's murderous anger forces him to flee. Blessed and commanded by Isaac not to marry a Canaanite, he goes to Paddan Aram, dreaming of a stairway to heaven at Bethel, where he receives the LORD's promises, sets up a pillar and makes a vow. He serves his uncle Laban twenty years: seven years for Rachel, whom he loves more than Leah, and who is replaced by Leah, then seven more for Rachel, then six for flocks under a wage agreement for speckled, spotted and black animals. Through his wives and their servants he fathers twelve sons and a daughter, Dinah, including Joseph and Benjamin by Rachel, and grows very wealthy in flocks, servants, camels and donkeys. Told by the LORD to return, he flees secretly, makes a covenant with Laban, and meets angels. Fearing Esau, he prays and sends gifts, then wrestles a man until daybreak, is renamed Israel, names Peniel and limps from a strained thigh. He reconciles with Esau, settles at Succoth and Shechem, buys land and erects the altar El Elohe Israel. He rebukes Simeon and Levi after the attack over Dinah, fearing his few numbers, and obeys God's call to Bethel, where God repeats the promise. Rachel dies after bearing Benjamin, and he later returns to bury Isaac with Esau. His favoritism for Joseph, shown by the tunic of many colors, leads to deep mourning when his sons deceive him with the bloodied tunic. Famine sends his sons to Egypt, and he fears for Benjamin. Learning Joseph lives, he goes to Egypt, receiving God's promise at Beersheba, and settles in Goshen. At 130 he tells Pharaoh his years were few and evil. He lives seventeen years in Egypt, adopts Ephraim and Manasseh, giving Joseph an extra portion, blesses his sons, charges them to bury him at Machpelah, and dies at 147, gathered to his people.
Abraham dies at a good old age of 175 and is gathered to his people; Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah in the Machpelah cave he purchased from the Hittites, after which God blesses Isaac.

was_exchanged_for stew (Jacob's red lentil stew) [sold by Esau] Jacob demanded Esau's birthright in exchange for food, and Esau, saying he was about to die and the birthright was no good to him, swore and sold it. The text concludes that Esau despised his birthright.
Red lentil stew boiled by Jacob; famished Esau asks for it, earning the name Edom, and trades his birthright to Jacob for bread and stew, then eats, drinks, and leaves.

Abimelech, Philistine king at Gerar, protects Isaac and his wife after rebuking him over calling her his sister, later sends him away as mightier, then comes with Ahuzzath and Phicol to seek a covenant, acknowledging Isaac's blessing by the LORD.

The wells dug in Abraham's days had been stopped and filled with earth by the Philistines, and Isaac digs them again and gives them their father's names. His servants' new wells are named Esek and Sitnah because of disputes, Rehoboth because there was no argument, and Shibah at Beersheba.

Abimelech, Ahuzzath, and Phicol propose an oath and covenant that Isaac will do them no harm, since they saw the LORD was with him and had done him only good. Isaac holds a feast, they swear an oath to one another the next morning, and they depart in peace.

Isaac's blessing of Jacob grants dew, fertile earth, grain, wine, service from nations, and lordship over his brothers, with curses and blessings on others. Being irrevocable, it leaves Esau a lesser blessing and breeds his hatred.

is_prepared_by Rebekah [for Isaac, as he loves] Isaac asks Esau to hunt venison and make savory food so that his soul may bless him. Rebekah instead prepares savory food from two young goats, as Isaac loves, and Jacob brings it to him with bread. Isaac eats it before Esau arrives with his own.

l: deception of Isaac (Jacob's impersonation of Esau), Genesis
s: Rebekah devises and Jacob performs an impersonation of Esau using his clothes and goat skins. Isaac notices Jacob's voice but accepts hairy hands and smell; the deceit is exposed when Esau arrives, and Isaac names it.
Jacob's dream stairway rests on earth with its top reaching heaven; angels of God ascend and descend on it, while the LORD stands above, speaking to Jacob.

l: stone pillar (Jacob's stone at Bethel), Genesis
s: A stone Jacob used as his pillow, then set up as a pillar and anointed with oil in the morning, which his vow declares will be God's house.

occurs_at Bethel [place where Jacob slept] While sleeping at a certain place after sunset, Jacob dreams of a stairway with angels ascending and descending and the LORD standing above it. The LORD gives promises of land, offspring, blessing and presence. Jacob wakes afraid, recognizing that the LORD is in the place and that it is the gate of heaven.

In Chapter 28, Jacob makes a conditional vow: if God is with him, protects him, provides bread and clothing, and returns him safely to his father's house, the LORD will be his God. He then promises that the stone pillar will be God's house and a tenth of everything.

previously_given_to Abraham [by God] The LORD promises Jacob the land on which he lies, for him and his offspring, and says he will bring him again into this land. Isaac's blessing likewise speaks of Jacob inheriting the land where he travels, which God gave to Abraham. The offspring are to spread west, east, north, and south.

Rachel is Laban's beautiful younger daughter, sister of Leah, and wife of Jacob, who loves her after meeting her at the well with her father's sheep. Barren at first, she envies Leah, demands children, and gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob; Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali, which Rachel names. She trades mandrakes for a night with Jacob, and God finally opens her womb, so she bears Joseph. She joins Leah in telling Jacob they have no portion in their father's house, then steals Laban's teraphim, hides them in a camel's saddle, and deceives him by claiming her period. Later, in hard labor on the way to Ephrath, she bears Benjamin, naming him Benoni, and dies. Jacob buries her on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem) and sets a pillar on her grave.

Leah is Laban's elder daughter, weak-eyed and less loved than Rachel, given to Jacob as his wife in Rachel's place. Seeing she is hated, the LORD opens her womb, and she bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, reading each birth in light of hoping for her husband's love. After she stops bearing, she gives her servant Zilpah to Jacob, then hires Jacob for a night with mandrakes, conceiving Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah. Finally, she joins Rachel in agreeing to leave Laban, who searches her tent for his gods without finding them.
Zilpah is Leah's servant, given by Laban to Leah, then by Leah to Jacob as a wife, bearing him two sons, Gad and Asher.
Bilhah, Rachel's servant and concubine given by Laban, is given to Jacob as wife by Rachel, then conceives and bears him two sons, Dan and Naphtali.

Reuben is Leah's son and Jacob's firstborn, with sons including Hanoch. He lies with his father's concubine Bilhah, and Israel hears of it. Later he opposes his brothers' plot to kill Joseph, urging them to throw him in a pit so he can restore him to his father; finding the pit empty, he tears his clothes in distress. Finally Jacob calls him his might and strength's beginning, but because he defiled his father's bed, declares him unstable and unable to excel.

Simeon is a son of Jacob and brother of Dinah and Levi, marked by violence. With Levi he kills the males of a city, including Hamor and Shechem, and Jacob rebukes them. Joseph later binds him as a hostage in Egypt until the youngest brother comes, and Jacob laments him. Finally Jacob condemns his and Levi's violent anger and declares they will be divided and scattered in Israel.

Levi, son of Jacob and brother of Dinah and Simeon, is violent. With Simeon he kills the males of a city, including Hamor and Shechem, to avenge Dinah, defying Jacob's rebuke. Later Jacob curses their cruel wrath and pronounces that Levi will be divided and scattered in Israel.

Judah is a son of Jacob (Israel) and brother of Joseph and Benjamin. The records follow him from a flawed early role to leadership and honor. In Chapter 37 he proposes selling Joseph to the Ishmaelites instead of killing him, and his brothers listen. In Chapter 38 he settles near his friend Hirah the Adullamite, marries Shua's daughter, and fathers Er, Onan, and Shelah. After Er and Onan die, he withholds Shelah from Er's widow Tamar, then unknowingly sleeps with her, leaving his signet, cord, and staff as a pledge. When she shows the pledge, he acknowledges she is more righteous than he. She bears twins, Perez and Zerah. In Chapter 43 he persuades Israel to send Benjamin to Egypt, offering himself as collateral and promising to bear the blame forever if he fails. In Chapter 44 he speaks for the brothers before Joseph, admits God has found out their iniquity, and offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place because of that pledge to his father. In Chapter 49 Jacob blesses him: his brothers will praise him and bow before him, he is a lion's cub, and the scepter will not depart from him.

l: well (in the field where Jacob met Rachel), Genesis
s: A well in a field in the land of the children of the east, used for watering flocks, its mouth covered by a large stone; three flocks wait there, and Jacob meets shepherds, then Rachel, and waters Laban's flock.

The large stone on the well's mouth is rolled away only when all the flocks are gathered, after which it is put back in its place. Jacob rolls it away himself to water Laban's flock when Rachel arrives.

l: seven years of service (Jacob for Rachel), Genesis
s: has_duration seven years [Jacob's service to Laban for Rachel] Jacob proposes to serve seven years for Rachel, and the years seem to him but a few days because of his love for her. When they are fulfilled, Laban gives him Leah instead, and Jacob must serve seven more years to receive Rachel as well.
Dinah, daughter of Leah and Jacob, goes out to see the land's daughters, is taken and humbled by Shechem, then is rescued from his house by brothers Simeon and Levi.
