Joseph is a Hebrew man, son of Jacob (Israel) in his old age, whose life moves from favored youth to slave, prisoner, and finally ruler of Egypt. At seventeen he is loved most by his father, given a tunic of many colors, and tells dreams of his family bowing to him. His brothers strip him, throw him into a pit, and sell him for twenty pieces of silver into Egypt, where Potiphar buys him. Because the LORD is with him, he prospers and becomes overseer of Potiphar's house. He refuses Potiphar's wife, saying it would be sin against God, but is falsely accused and imprisoned. There he again gains favor with the keeper and is put in charge of the prisoners, including Pharaoh's chief cup bearer and chief baker. He says interpretations belong to God and interprets their dreams; the cup bearer forgets him, though Joseph claims he was stolen from the land of the Hebrews and is innocent. Brought before Pharaoh at thirty, he interprets the dreams of cattle as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine and advises storing grain. Pharaoh sets him over Egypt, gives him a signet ring, the name Zaphenath-Paneah, and Asenath as wife; she bears Manasseh and Ephraim. He sells grain during the famine. When his brothers come, he recognizes them, acts as a stranger, accuses them of spying, keeps Simeon bound, and weeps privately. He tests them with Benjamin, favors Benjamin at the meal, and plants his silver cup in Benjamin's sack, claiming to practice divination. He then reveals himself, saying God sent him ahead to preserve life and made him father to Pharaoh and ruler of Egypt. He gives gifts, including silver and clothing to Benjamin, brings Jacob's family to Goshen, and provides them bread. He acquires the money, livestock, and land of the Egyptians for Pharaoh, and sets a fifth of the harvest as Pharaoh's due. He swears to bury Jacob in his fathers' burying place, and objects when Jacob lays his right hand on Ephraim. Jacob calls him a fruitful vine, strengthened by the Mighty One of Jacob, separated from his brothers. After burying Jacob in Canaan, he reassures his fearful brothers that God meant their evil for good and promises to provide for them, showing a forgiving, kind disposition. He lives 110 years, sees Ephraim's children to the third generation, makes Israel's children swear to carry up his bones, and is embalmed and placed in a coffin in Egypt.

split_into feebler to Laban, stronger to Jacob [result of Jacob's breeding practice] The flocks increased from little to a multitude under Jacob's care. After the spotted and dark animals are removed, the flocks conceive in front of the peeled rods and produce streaked, speckled, and spotted young, with the stronger ones becoming Jacob's and the feebler Laban's.
Rods of fresh poplar, almond and plane tree, peeled with white streaks, are set by Jacob in the watering troughs before the flocks, which then conceive and bear streaked, speckled and spotted young.

l: wages agreement (Jacob and Laban's hire), Genesis
s: A hire agreement in which Jacob declines set payment and asks for speckled, spotted and black animals as wages, with unmarked animals found with him counted stolen; Laban agrees, and Jacob's flocks greatly increase.

l: children (Rachel and Jacob's wives' children), Genesis
s: Through Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah, and Rachel, Jacob has sons Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, and Joseph, plus a daughter, Dinah, along with Reuben, who is already Leah's son. Their names are given with explanations tied to the rivalry between Rachel and Leah.

is_a household gods Rachel steals Laban's teraphim while he is shearing sheep. Laban accuses Jacob of stealing them, and Jacob, not knowing Rachel took them, says whoever has them shall not live. Rachel hides them in the camel's saddle and sits on them, so Laban's search of the tents does not find them.

Jacob's family, a shepherding household descended through Leah, Zilpah, Rachel and Bilhah; sixty-six direct offspring entered Egypt, with Joseph's two Egypt-born sons making seventy, planning to settle in Goshen.

Jacob tells Rachel and Leah that the flock bore speckled and streaked young according to the wages Laban named, and that God has taken Laban's livestock and given it to him. Jacob takes all his livestock, including what he gained in Paddan Aram, when he leaves, and says he bore the losses of torn animals during his years of service.

is_a mountain Gilead is the mountain toward which Jacob sets his face after crossing the River. Laban overtakes him there after seven days, and both camp in the mountain, where God warns Laban in a dream and where the covenant is made.

A heap of stones in the mountain of Gilead, gathered by Jacob's relatives beside his pillar after a shared meal. Named Jegar Sahadutha by Laban, Galeed by Jacob, and Mizpah, it witnesses that neither man will cross it to harm the other.

l: covenant between Jacob and Laban, Genesis
s: A covenant Laban proposes to Jacob as a witness between them: Jacob must not afflict Laban's daughters or take other wives, and neither may cross the heap and pillar to harm the other, with God as judge. Jacob swears, sacrifices, and shares a meal.

Jacob's secret flight from Laban: after the LORD's command and his wives' agreement, he leaves for Canaan and Isaac without telling Laban. Laban pursues and overtakes him in Gilead, accuses him over the stolen gods, searches fruitlessly, and the confrontation ends in a covenant.

Jacob's present for Esau is a large gift of livestock: goats, ewes, rams, milk camels with colts, cows, bulls, donkeys and foals. Jacob has servants drive it in separate herds ahead of him, telling Esau it is Jacob's gift, to appease him. Later Jacob explains it was meant to find favor. Esau first refuses, saying he has enough, but Jacob insists and Esau accepts.

The sons of Jacob are summoned to assemble and hear their father's words about their future. Each receives his own blessing, and they are then instructed to bury Jacob with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah.

An unnamed man wrestles Jacob at the Jabbok until daybreak, strains Jacob's thigh when he cannot prevail, renames him Israel for fighting God and men, blesses him, and refuses to disclose his own name.

Jacob, left alone at the Jabbok ford after crossing his family, wrestles a man until daybreak. His thigh is strained, he demands a blessing and receives the name Israel. The place is named Peniel; Jacob limps, explaining the hip-sinew prohibition.

Jacob divides the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two servants, with the servants' children in front, Leah's next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear. Jacob tells Esau they are the children God has graciously given him, and each group comes near and bows before Esau. Jacob later cites their tenderness as the reason for traveling slowly.

is_a Hivite Hamor, father of Shechem, goes out to Jacob and proposes intermarriage, shared land, and trade. He accepts the circumcision condition and persuades the men at the city gate, arguing that Jacob's livestock and possessions would become theirs, and is later killed by Simeon and Levi.

l: reconciliation of Jacob and Esau, Genesis
s: involves Esau [embraced and wept with Jacob] Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces and kisses him, and the two weep, showing a peaceful meeting where Jacob had approached with deference. Esau accepts the gift and offers to accompany Jacob, but Jacob asks to follow at his own pace toward Seir. The brothers then part, with Esau returning to Seir and Jacob traveling to Succoth.

Shechem, honored prince of the land and son of Hamor the Hivite, takes Dinah, then loves her and seeks her as wife, offering any dowry and accepting circumcision, but is killed by the sword along with his father.

are_sons_of Jacob Jacob's sons come in from the field grieved and very angry that folly was done in Israel. They answer Shechem and Hamor with deceit, demanding circumcision, and afterward plunder the city, taking its animals, wealth, women, and little ones.

are circumcised [after consenting to Hamor and Shechem] The men who went out of the city gate listen to Hamor and Shechem and every male is circumcised, persuaded by the prospect of peace, intermarriage, and gaining the newcomers' livestock and possessions. On the third day, while sore, all the males are killed by Simeon and Levi.

The city, whose gate is the site of Hamor and Shechem's address to its men, is come upon unsuspecting on the third day after the circumcision. It is plundered of its flocks, herds, donkeys, wealth, and houses' contents, and its wives and little ones are taken captive.

Israel, also called Jacob, is an aged father who worships God Almighty and has sons by his wife Rachel, including Benjamin, whose life he loves as bound up with his own. In Chapter 43 he reluctantly yields to Judah's pledge and sends Benjamin with a present, double money, and a prayer for mercy, resigning himself to possible bereavement. In Chapter 44, Judah recounts his grief over a lost son and fear that losing another would bring his gray hairs down to Sheol. In Chapter 50 he is embalmed by Joseph's physicians, mourned seventy days by the Egyptians, and buried by his sons at the cave of Machpelah, as he wished. His brothers claim he asked that Joseph forgive them.

is_practiced_by sons of Jacob [condition for intermarriage] Jacob's sons set circumcision of every male as the condition for giving and taking daughters and becoming one people, calling an uncircumcised husband a reproach. The city's males all undergo it, and on the third day, while they are sore, they are killed.

perpetrated_by Shechem Shechem's taking and lying with Dinah is called defiling her, and it provokes grief and anger in Jacob's sons as folly in Israel, a thing that ought not to be done. It is given as the reason for their deceitful answer and for the plunder, and the sons cite it in their final reply to Jacob.

l: massacre and plunder of the city, Genesis
s: Simeon and Levi slaughter the city's males, including Hamor and Shechem, and retrieve Dinah; Jacob's sons then plunder livestock, wealth, houses, and capture women and children, leaving Jacob fearing retaliation.

Benjamin is the youngest son of Jacob, born to Rachel during her fatal labor on the way to Ephrath. Rachel named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin. He is Joseph's full brother, and Jacob, who loves him as the child of his old age, keeps him home after Joseph is presumed dead, calling him the only one left of his mother's sons. Joseph demands that Benjamin be brought to Egypt to prove the brothers' honesty. Jacob yields after Judah pledges to answer for him. Joseph blesses him, weeps, and gives him a portion five times larger than the others'. Joseph's silver cup is then found in Benjamin's sack, and Joseph declares he will become a slave, prompting Judah's speech.

is_a death [old and full of days] Isaac dies at the age of one hundred eighty after Jacob has come to him at Mamre (Hebron). He gives up the spirit and is gathered to his people, old and full of days, and his sons Esau and Jacob bury him.

is_a hard labor ending in death [on the way to Ephrath] On the journey from Bethel, some distance short of Ephrath, Rachel goes into hard labor, and the midwife reassures her that she will have another son. She dies as she gives birth, naming the boy Benoni while Jacob names him Benjamin. She is buried on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem), and Jacob marks her grave with a pillar.

Edom is identified as another name for Esau, who lived in the hill country of Seir. The land of Edom is where the chiefs of Eliphaz, Reuel, and the Horites are said to have come from, and where kings reigned before any king reigned over Israel.

The Edomites are descendants of Esau in Seir's hill country, traced through Eliphaz, Reuel, and Oholibamah's sons, with chiefs listed (Timna, Alvah, Teman, Kenaz and others), ending with chiefs by habitation.

is_a twin son of Tamar [born second, with scarlet thread on hand] Zerah is Tamar's other twin son by Judah. His hand comes out first and the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it, but he is born after Perez.

A list of eight kings who reigned in Edom before any king ruled Israel. Each succeeded the one who died, beginning with Bela son of Beor at Dinhabah and ending with Hadar. Notable details: Hadad struck Midian in the field of Moab, and Hadar's wife was Mehetabel.

Joseph's brothers, including Benjamin, hate and envy him over their father's favoritism and his dreams. At Dothan they plot to kill him, strip his tunic, throw him in a pit, and sell him to traders into Egypt, deceiving Jacob with a bloodied tunic. Later, terrified when Joseph reveals himself, they are reassured, reconciled, and carry the news to Jacob in Canaan.

is_a caravan [from Gilead, trading spices, balm and myrrh to Egypt] A caravan of Ishmaelites comes from Gilead with camels bearing spices, balm, and myrrh, going down to Egypt. Joseph is sold to them for twenty pieces of silver.

is_a merchants Midianite merchants pass by, draw Joseph up out of the pit, and sell him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver, bringing him into Egypt. They are also said to have sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh.

Potiphar is an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, married to Potiphar's wife. He buys Joseph, sees the LORD is with him, and is blessed for Joseph's sake. He entrusts everything to Joseph except his food, but after his wife's accusation, he angrily imprisons Joseph.

Israel makes the tunic of many colors for Joseph, which marks his favored status and fuels his brothers' hatred. The brothers strip it from him at Dothan, dip it in goat's blood, and bring it to Jacob as false evidence that Joseph was killed, and Jacob recognizes it.

Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves bow to his sheaf, and then that the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to him. His brothers hate him all the more and his father rebukes him, though Jacob keeps the saying in mind; the brothers later mock him as "this dreamer" and say they will see what becomes of his dreams.

has_state empty [no water in it] The pit in the wilderness is empty, with no water, and is where the brothers throw Joseph after stripping him. Reuben intends it to keep Joseph alive, and the merchants later draw Joseph out of it, so Reuben finds it empty on his return.

has_price twenty pieces of silver [sold to the Ishmaelites] On Judah's proposal, Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver to the Ishmaelites by passing Midianite merchants, who lift him out of the pit and bring him to Egypt. The brothers conceal the sale with a goat's-blood-stained tunic, and Joseph is ultimately sold to Potiphar.

Tamar is a woman widowed when her husband Er dies. Judah sends her to live in her father's house as a widow until Shelah grows up. When he is withheld from her, she veils herself, conceives by Judah, and keeps his pledge. Condemned, she proves him the father, is declared more righteous, and bears twins Perez and Zerah.
Er, Judah's firstborn son and Onan's brother, was married to Tamar, was wicked in the LORD's sight, and was killed by the LORD in Canaan.

Onan is Judah's second son, obliged to raise offspring for his brother Er's widow Tamar. Knowing the child wouldn't be his, he spilled his semen on the ground. This was evil in the LORD's sight, and the LORD killed him in Canaan.
Perez, twin son of Tamar and Judah, is born after his brother Zerah's hand appears; the midwife says he made a breach, naming him. He fathers Hezron and Hamul.

is_located_on way to Timnah [has a gate] Enaim is a place on the way to Timnah with a gate where Tamar sits veiled and meets Judah. When Judah's friend asks the men there about a prostitute, they say none has been there.

l: pledge (Judah's signet, cord and staff), Genesis
s: consists_of signet, cord and staff [given by Judah to Tamar] Judah gives his signet, cord, and staff to the veiled Tamar as a pledge until he sends a young goat. His friend cannot find her to redeem it, and Judah lets her keep it. Tamar later sends the items to him as proof of the father of her child, and Judah acknowledges them.

l: Levirate duty (duty of a husband's brother), Genesis
s: requires raising offspring for deceased brother [by going in to brother's widow] Judah commands Onan to go in to Er's widow Tamar and perform the duty of a husband's brother to raise up offspring for Er. Onan evades it and is killed. Judah then withholds Shelah from fulfilling it, which he later admits was wrong.

Potiphar's wife, married to Potiphar, repeatedly urges Joseph to lie with her. When he flees leaving his garment, she summons her household and falsely accuses him of attempted assault, keeping the garment as evidence until her husband returns.

The prison is a place for the king's prisoners, located in the house of the captain of the guard. Joseph is bound there in custody, then given charge of all prisoners. Pharaoh's cup bearer and baker are also held there, while Joseph insists he did nothing wrong.

delegates_to Joseph [does not look after anything under Joseph's hand] The keeper of the prison, favorably disposed to Joseph through the LORD's doing, commits all the prisoners to Joseph's hand. He does not look after anything under Joseph's care because the LORD is with Joseph and makes his work prosper.

is_owned_by Joseph [left in her hand and kept as supposed evidence] Joseph leaves his garment in the hand of Potiphar's wife when she catches him and he runs outside. She keeps it beside her and uses it as supposed evidence in her account to the men of her house and to Potiphar.

l: false accusation of attempted assault, Genesis
s: Potiphar's wife falsely claims Joseph tried to lie with her, using his left garment as proof after he fled; Potiphar, enraged, imprisons Joseph despite his having refused her.

The chief cup bearer offends Pharaoh and is jailed with the chief baker. Joseph interprets his vine dream, predicting restoration within three days. On Pharaoh's birthday he is restored to his position, but he forgets Joseph.

The chief baker offends Pharaoh and is imprisoned, then tells Joseph his dream of three bread baskets eaten by birds. Joseph interprets it as death within three days, and Pharaoh hangs him on his birthday.
A dream in Chapter 40 of a vine with three branches that buds and ripens into grapes the cup bearer presses into Pharaoh's cup; Joseph interprets the branches as three days until restoration.

belongs_to God [per Joseph] Joseph asks whether interpretations belong to God before hearing the dreams, then gives the cup bearer a favorable interpretation and the baker an unfavorable one. Both are fulfilled on the third day, as the text states when it says the baker was hanged as Joseph had interpreted.

l: Pharaoh's dream of the cattle, Genesis
s: symbolizes seven years of plenty and famine [seven good cattle are plenty, seven thin cattle are famine] In this dream Pharaoh stands by the river and sees seven sleek, fat cattle come up and feed in the marsh grass, followed by seven ugly, thin cattle that eat them up and remain as ugly as before. Joseph explains that the seven good cattle are seven years of plenty and the seven thin cattle are seven years of famine.
